newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia moves to regain control over arms trade.
newsitem.headline: Russia moves to regain control over arms trade.

text.p: The Russian parliament passed a law on Friday designed to reassert state control over weapons exports and stop arms being sold on world markets at what one deputy called "dumping prices".

The collapse of centralised controls after the Soviet Union fell apart in 1991 led to chaos in the arms industry. Moscow lost its postition on world arms markets while weapons flooded out of the country bypassing government controls and taxes.
Pavel Sazhinov, a member of the upper house of parliament's defence commitee, told the chamber the state's share of earnings from arms trading had plunged over the past five years.

"Many firms began offering military equipment and weapons at prices significantly lower than those offered by the state," said Sazhinov, who also heads the local legislature in the northern port of Murmansk.
"Every year the treasury loses $1 billion because firms trade abroad directly...We have basically been trading on world markets at dumping prices."
The United States has taken advantage of Russia's post-communist political and economic weakness to boost its share of the arms market in recent years.

Western Europe has also been conducting a hard-sell campaign on the former Soviet bloc states who will be looking to bring their arms into line with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, which most want to join. Several will be invited to join the western defence alliance at the end of this month.
But Moscow is trying to fight back, partly by stepping in where political considerations keep U.S. firms away.

In one recent example, Indonesia stepped up negotiations with Russia on buying Sukhoi-30 and MiG-29 fighters, radar, guided missiles and helicopters after cancelling a plan to buy U.S. F-16s in May because of congressional criticism in Washington.

Indonesian Research and Technology Minister Jusuf Habibie is at present visiting Russia and Indonesia's air force chief of staff, Sutria Tubagus, inspected the aircraft last month at the Paris Air Show.
President Boris Yeltsin on Friday underlined the show's importance as a symbol of the revival of its arms industry.
"Just take the recent air show in France. There our producers' achievements literally shook the world," President Boris Yelstin said during a nationwide radio address.
"In August we will have a Russian air show at Zhukovo -- showing once again what Russia is capable of," he added.

In a further boost to Russian pride, Friday's Izvestia daily frontpaged a report that the Mig-25 had broken a world altitude record. "It won't rock the country but the arms traders are satisfied," the paper said.
Sazhinov said the government set great store by the arms trade law, which the upper house of parliament or Federation Council then passed by 115 votes to three, paving the way for Yelstin to sign it.
One regional leader had complained that the state arms trader Rosvooruzhenie had got in the way of a firm in his region's attempt to sell its output abroad.
Sazhinov replied that while the law reasserted a state monopoly over arms trading and excluded what he called "unfair" competition between firms, it did not allow a monopoly by one organisation.
